turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi, thanks for coming in today. What's been going on for you lately?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: It's been fine, I guess. Just a lot on my plate at work and trying to keep up with everything. I mean, it's not like it's anything out of the ordinary. Just the usual stuff. (pauses)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now, even if a part of you feels like you *should* be used to it. Sometimes, even the "usual stuff" can get exhausting when it feels like a constant effort just to keep up.

I noticed you paused at the end there. How heavy is that plate feeling for you right now, under the surface?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (slightly defensive) Oh, it's not that heavy, really. I just... (pauses again, choosing words carefully) ...I just feel like I'm always on edge, you know? Like I'm waiting for something to go wrong. (shrugs)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
I really appreciate you sharing that with me, especially when it feels a bit uncomfortable to put into words. 

That feeling of being "on edge"—like you're constantly bracing yourself, waiting for the other shoe to drop—is incredibly exhausting. It’s like running a background program on your computer that never turns off; even if you think you *should* be able to handle it, it drains your battery. 

Living in that state of constant alert is a heavy thing to carry, even if you're used to pushing through it. 

When you're in that "on edge" mode day-to-day, how does it show up for you? Is it more of a physical tension, racing thoughts, or something else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (hesitates, seemingly unsure how to answer) It's... it's just kind of a... a nagging feeling, I guess. Like, I'll be doing something completely normal, and then suddenly I'll just feel this... this urge to do something else, too. Like, I'll be getting ready to leave the house, and I'll need to... do this thing. (pauses again)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
I hear how carefully you're choosing your words, and I want to reassure you that there's no "right" way to describe this. It takes a lot of courage to talk about things that feel hard to explain.

What you're describing—that sudden, compelling urge to "do a thing" right in the middle of a normal routine—is actually very common, especially when someone has been living with that high "on edge" feeling for a while. It’s almost like your brain creates a little rule or a pit stop that you have to complete before you can move on.

Does doing "this thing" feel like it temporarily calms down that nagging feeling, or does it feel more like a demand your brain is making that you just have to follow? 

You can share as much or as little about what that "thing" is whenever you feel ready—there's zero judgment here.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (gets slightly more agitated, but still trying to be careful with words) It's not like it calms me down or anything. It's more like... I need to do it to, you know, feel okay. If I don't do it, I'll just feel this... this anxiety building up inside me, and I'll get more and more... (pauses, trying to find the right words) ...on edge. It's like my brain is just telling me that I have to do it, and if I don't, there'll be consequences or something. (looks down, fidgeting slightly)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
First, I want to pause and thank you for trusting me enough to share that. I can see how uncomfortable and stressful this is to talk about—it makes total sense that you'd feel a bit agitated or want to look away. Talking about these things can feel really vulnerable, and there's often a lot of quiet shame attached to them. You are doing a really brave thing by putting words to it today.

What you just described is actually a very classic and deeply human cycle. 

Your brain registers a threat—that background "on edge" feeling—and it gives you a rule: *"If you do this specific thing, you will prevent the anxiety from exploding, and you'll stay safe."* So doing "the thing" isn't necessarily about joy or real calm; it's about keeping the lid on a pot that feels like it's about to boil over. 

It makes complete sense why you feel compelled to do it. Your brain is trying to protect you from that overwhelming, building panic. But living like that—having to follow these rigid rules just to prevent a disaster or a huge spike in anxiety—is exhausting. 

How long has your brain been setting these kinds of rules for you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (gets slightly more comfortable, but still guarded) I don't know... it feels like it's always been this way, but I guess it's been getting worse over the past year or so. It's hard to pinpoint when it started, to be honest. (pauses, looking down) I just feel like I'm always trying to keep this thing under control, you know? And it's not just the one thing... it's multiple things. And if I don't do them, I feel like I'm not going to be able to... (stops, taking a deep breath) ...handle it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Take a deep breath. You are doing incredible work right now, just letting those words out. 

It makes complete sense that you feel exhausted. You came in talking about having "a lot on your plate at work," but the reality is, you’ve been working *two* full-time jobs: your actual job, and this constant, demanding job inside your mind of managing these rules and trying to keep the anxiety at bay. No wonder it feels like a heavy load.

What you just touched on is so important: *"If I don't do them, I feel like I'm not going to be able to handle it."* 

Your brain has convinced you that if you don't follow these steps, the wave of anxiety that follows will be so massive, so intolerable, that it will crush you or outlast your ability to cope. So doing "the things" becomes a survival mechanism—a way to protect yourself from a feeling that feels bottomless.

I want you to know that what you're describing—this cycle where anxiety makes demands, and fulfilling them keeps you trapped in high alert—is something we understand very well in therapy. You are not crazy, you are not weak, and you don't have to keep carrying this completely alone.

When you think about that feeling of "not being able to handle it," what does that actually feel like to you? Is it a fear of the anxiety itself getting too intense, or a fear that something bad will actually happen if you stop?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (gets slightly more emotional, but still trying to hold back) It feels like... it feels like I'm drowning, I guess. Like, I'm standing in the middle of a storm, and if I stop moving, the water will just keep rising, and I'll go under. (pauses, taking a deep breath) It's not just the anxiety itself, it's the feeling that I'll lose control. That I'll make a mistake, or forget something, or... (trails off, looking down) I don't know, it's just this constant feeling of being on the edge of disaster, and if I don't keep moving, it'll all come crashing down. (looks up, eyes welling up)

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
I see how painful this is, and I am so glad you're letting yourself feel that right now. You’ve been holding that storm inside for a really long time, trying so hard to keep it from leaking out. 

That image you just shared—standing in the middle of a storm, feeling like if you stop moving for even a second, the water will swallow you up—captures the absolute terror and exhaustion of living this way so powerfully. It makes total sense why you feel so worn down. 

Your brain has convinced you that these "things" you do are the only life raft keeping disaster at bay—keeping you from losing control or making a mistake that feels fatal. When you believe the water is always rising, of course you keep swimming as fast as you can.

I want to tell you something really important: you aren't struggling because you're weak or broken. You feel like you're drowning because you've been trying to survive a hurricane all by yourself, using every ounce of your energy just to keep your head above water.

You don't have to carry the storm alone anymore. Therapy is a place where we can work together to help you realize that you *can* stop running, and the water won't swallow you whole. 

How does it feel right now, in this room, to finally pause for a moment and say all of this out loud?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (breaks down in tears, feeling a mix of relief and exhaustion) It feels... (pauses, trying to find the words) ...it feels like a weight has been lifted, I guess. Like, I've been carrying this around for so long, and it's finally okay to say out loud that it's too much. That I'm tired. That I need help. (sobs) It's just... it's so hard to explain, but it feels like I've been living in this constant state of emergency, and finally, I can see that it's not real. That I'm not drowning, I'm just... (pauses, taking a deep breath) ...I'm just trying to survive.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
Just take your time. Let those tears fall—they have been waiting to come out for a very long time. You don't have to hold it together here.

Hearing you say *"I'm tired,"* and *"I need help"* isn't a sign of weakness or defeat. It is actually the moment you start taking your power back. It takes immense strength to stop fighting the reality of how exhausted you are and just admit that it's too much.

And what you just realized is so incredibly profound: *You were living in a constant state of emergency, but the emergency wasn't real—you were just trying to survive.* 

Your brain wasn't broken; it was just terrified, using every rule and routine it could think of to keep you safe. But you don't have to live in emergency mode forever. Now that we’ve named it, we can slowly, step-by-step, start teaching your nervous system that you *are* safe, and that you don't have to keep running just to stay afloat.

I am right here with you. You don't have to do this by yourself anymore.

How does your body feel right now, in this moment, as you let some of that weight go?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (sobs uncontrollably, feeling a mix of emotions) My body... (pauses, trying to catch her breath) ...my body feels... (pauses again) ...it feels like it's finally allowed to relax. Like, my shoulders aren't holding up the weight of the world anymore. My muscles aren't tense, and my jaw isn't clenched. (starts to calm down, taking deep breaths) I feel... (pauses once more) ...I feel like I'm slowly coming back to myself. Like, I'm remembering who I am outside of this constant state of emergency. (looks up, eyes red from crying) It's... (smiles slightly) ...it's a weird feeling, but it's also kind of... (pauses, searching for the right word) ...liberating?

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
"Liberating" is a beautiful word for it. 

Look at what just happened: the moment you allowed yourself to stop fighting, to stop carrying the weight of the world on your own, your body knew exactly what to do. Your shoulders dropped, your jaw unclenched, and you took a full, real breath. 

That part of you—the real you outside of the rules, the anxiety, and the constant vigilance—has been right there the whole time, waiting for a safe space to come back out. 

This is what it feels like when your brain and body finally get the message: *The emergency is over for right now. We are safe.*

It might feel a little strange or unfamiliar because you've been in "survival mode" for so long, but this feeling of ease? *This* is your baseline. This is who you are when you're not forced to be a soldier in a war inside your head.

We have plenty of work ahead of us to help you build tools so you can access this peace out in the real world, but for today, you did something huge. You broke the cycle just by being honest with yourself.

How does it feel to just sit here with that liberated feeling for a few moments, without needing to rush to the next thing?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (smiles softly, feeling a sense of peace) It feels... (pauses, savoring the moment) ...it feels like I'm home. Like, I'm finally in a place where I can just be myself, without all the extra weight and worry. (closes her eyes, taking a deep breath) It's like I can feel my heart beating in a different way. Like, it's not racing or pounding or trying to escape. It's just... (opens her eyes, looking at the therapist) ...it's just beating. (smiles again) It's a really nice feeling.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
That is so profound. "It feels like I'm home." 

Notice that—your body already knows what safety feels like. A heart that isn't pounding or trying to escape, but just beating steadily, doing its job with ease. 

That "home" you're describing isn't just this room—it's a state inside of *you* that you just reconnected with. You brought yourself here today, you had the courage to drop the heavy armor, and you gave yourself permission to step back into your own life.

This is a really powerful milestone. The anxiety and the rules might try to whisper to you again in the days ahead—that's normal, because habits take time to rewire—but now you have a reference point. You know what it feels like to land safely back in yourself.

As we get ready to wrap up today, take another slow breath and just let your body absorb this calm. 

How are you feeling about stepping back out into your day, carrying a little bit of this "home" feeling with you?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: (smiles, feeling a sense of hope and possibility) I'm... (pauses, thinking) ...I'm feeling a little bit lighter, I think. Like, I can actually imagine making it through the day without feeling like I'm going to lose my head. (laughs softly) It's funny, I was really worried about what would happen if I stopped fighting, but it turns out... it's not the end of the world. (smiles again) In fact, it feels kind of... (pauses, searching for the right word) ...freeing. Like, I can finally start to imagine a life that's not just about surviving.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text:
That soft laugh says so much. It really is the ultimate paradox, isn't it? Anxiety tries to convince us that if we drop our guard, everything will collapse. But when you actually give yourself permission to let go of that impossible grip, you discover that the ground beneath you was solid all along.

Shifting your goal from *surviving* to actually *living* is a huge, beautiful turning point. You don't just have to manage your days anymore—you get to experience them, enjoy them, and be present in your own life.

Of course, this is a practice, and there will still be moments where that old "emergency alarm" tries to go off. But today, you proved to yourself that the panic doesn't get the final say. You have a new way forward now.

As you head out today, see if you can carry just a piece of this lightness with you. You don't have to rush, and you don't have to carry the weight of the world anymore. Just take it one step, and one breath, at a time.

I’m really proud of the courageous work you did here today. How are you feeling about ending our session here for now?
